question: If \(a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots\) are in A.P. such that \(a_1+a_7+a_{16}=40\), find the sum of the first 15 terms.
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(S_{15}=15a_8\) since \(a_8\) is the middle (8th) term of 15 — spot that the middle term times the count gives the sum directly.

question: Let \(a_n\) be the nth term of a G.P. of positive terms. If \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{100}a_{2n+1}=200\) and \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{100}a_{2n}=100\), find \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{200}a_n\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: In a GP, shifting every index by \(k\) multiplies the corresponding sum by \(r^k\) — use that ratio between the two given sums to find \(r\) before touching anything else.
subject: math

question: \[\sum_{n=1}^{21}\frac{3}{(4n-1)(4n+3)}\]
solution: \(\dfrac1{4n-1}-\dfrac1{4n+3}=\dfrac{4}{(4n-1)(4n+3)}\), so \(\dfrac{3}{(4n-1)(4n+3)}=\dfrac34\left(\dfrac1{4n-1}-\dfrac1{4n+3}\right)\).The sum telescopes: \(\dfrac34\left(\dfrac13-\dfrac1{87}\right)=\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac{84}{261}=\dfrac{7}{29}\)
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Spot that \((4n+3)-(4n-1)=4\) — that constant gap is exactly what turns the product into a clean telescoping difference.
subject: math

question: If \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt1+\sqrt2}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2+\sqrt3}+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{99}+\sqrt{100}}=m\) and \(\dfrac{1}{1\cdot2}+\dfrac{1}{2\cdot3}+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{99\cdot100}=n\), find \(m\) and \(n\).
solution: Rationalizing each term of \(m\): \(\dfrac1{\sqrt k+\sqrt{k+1}}=\sqrt{k+1}-\sqrt k\), so \(m\) telescopes to \(\sqrt{100}-\sqrt1=10-1=9\).For \(n\): \(\dfrac1{k(k+1)}=\dfrac1k-\dfrac1{k+1}\), so \(n=1-\dfrac1{100}=\dfrac{99}{100}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Both sums are telescoping in disguise — one needs rationalizing the surd first, the other needs a partial-fraction split first.
subject: math

question: If the sum of the first 20 terms of the series \(\log_{7^{1/2}}x+\log_{7^{1/3}}x+\log_{7^{1/4}}x+\cdots\) is 460, find \(x\).
solution: Using \(\log_{a^{1/k}}b=k\log_ab\), the \(k\)th term (starting \(k=1\)) is \(\log_{7^{1/(k+1)}}x=(k+1)\log_7x\), so for \(k=1,\ldots,20\) the coefficients run \(2,3,\ldots,21\).\[\text{Sum}=\log_7x\left(\sum_{j=2}^{21}j\right)=\log_7x\,(230)=460\Rightarrow\log_7x=2\Rightarrow x=49\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: \(\log_{a^{1/k}}b=k\log_ab\) turns a scary log series into an ordinary arithmetic sum of integers multiplying a single constant \(\log_7x\).
subject: math

question: The sum of the first 20 terms of the series \(5+11+19+29+41+\cdots\) is:
solution: Differences are \(6,8,10,12,\ldots\) (an AP with \(d=2\)), so the general term is quadratic. Summing the differences from \(a_1=5\): \(a_n=5+(n-1)(n+4)=n^2+3n+1\).\[S_{20}=\sum_{n=1}^{20}(n^2+3n+1)=\frac{20\cdot21\cdot41}{6}+3\cdot\frac{20\cdot21}{2}+20=2870+630+20=3520\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Constant second differences signal a quadratic \(a_n\) — rebuild \(a_n\) from the differences first, then sum with the standard \(\sum n,\sum n^2\) formulas.
subject: math

question: If \(A=\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\big(3+(-1)^n\big)^n}\) and \(B=\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{\big(3+(-1)^n\big)^n}\), find \(\dfrac AB\).
solution: Split by parity. For even \(n\): denominator is \(4^n\), and both \(A,B\) get \(+\tfrac1{4^n}\). For odd \(n\): denominator is \(2^n\), \(A\) gets \(+\tfrac1{2^n}\) but \(B\) gets \(-\tfrac1{2^n}\).\(\displaystyle\sum_{\text{even }n\ge2}\frac1{4^n}=\frac{1/16}{1-1/16}=\frac1{15}\), \(\displaystyle\sum_{\text{odd }n\ge1}\frac1{2^n}=\frac{1/2}{1-1/4}=\frac23\).\[A=\frac1{15}+\frac23=\frac{11}{15},\quad B=\frac1{15}-\frac23=-\frac35\Rightarrow\frac AB=\frac{11/15}{-3/5}=-\frac{11}{9}\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Split any series with \((-1)^n\) inside a more complex expression into its even-index and odd-index halves — each half is a plain GP.
subject: math

question: If the sum of the first \(n\) terms of an A.P. is \(cn^2\), find the sum of the squares of these \(n\) terms.
solution: \(a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=cn^2-c(n-1)^2=c(2n-1)\), so this is an AP with first term \(c\) and common difference \(2c\).\[\sum_{k=1}^n a_k^2=c^2\sum_{k=1}^n(2k-1)^2=c^2\cdot\frac{n(2n-1)(2n+1)}{3}=\frac{c^2n(4n^2-1)}3\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Recover the general term with \(a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\) first — don't try to guess the AP's first term and common difference from \(S_n\) directly.
subject: math

question: Find the harmonic mean of the roots of \((5+\sqrt2)x^2-(4+\sqrt5)x+(8+2\sqrt5)=0\).
solution: For roots \(\alpha,\beta\): sum \(=-b/a=\dfrac{4+\sqrt5}{5+\sqrt2}\), product \(=c/a=\dfrac{8+2\sqrt5}{5+\sqrt2}\). Since \(8+2\sqrt5=2(4+\sqrt5)\):\[\text{HM}=\frac{2\alpha\beta}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac{2c}{-b}=\frac{2(8+2\sqrt5)}{4+\sqrt5}=\frac{4(4+\sqrt5)}{4+\sqrt5}=4\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: HM of the roots of \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) is always \(\dfrac{2c}{-b}\) — a one-line formula, no need to solve for the roots themselves.
subject: math

question: The third term of a G.P. is 4. Find the product of its first five terms.
solution: \(a_3=ar^2=4\). The product of 5 consecutive GP terms centered on \(a_3\) is \((a_3)^5\) (each pair equidistant from the center multiplies to \(a_3^2\)):\[a\cdot ar\cdot ar^2\cdot ar^3\cdot ar^4=a^5r^{10}=(ar^2)^5=4^5=1024\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: The product of an odd number of consecutive GP terms is just the middle term raised to that count — skip multiplying out all five factors.
subject: math

question: The sides of a right-angled triangle are in arithmetic progression. If the triangle has area 24, find the length of its smallest side.
solution: Write the sides as \(a-d,\,a,\,a+d\) with hypotenuse \(a+d\). Pythagoras: \((a-d)^2+a^2=(a+d)^2\Rightarrow a^2=4ad\Rightarrow a=4d\).So the sides are \(3d,4d,5d\) (a scaled 3-4-5 triangle). Area \(=\tfrac12(3d)(4d)=6d^2=24\Rightarrow d=2\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Writing AP sides as \(a-d,a,a+d\) and applying Pythagoras forces \(a=4d\) immediately — recognize the 3-4-5 shape before touching the area condition.
subject: math

question: Let \(X\) be the set of the first 2018 terms of the A.P. \(1,6,11,\ldots\) and \(Y\) be the set of the first 2018 terms of the A.P. \(9,16,23,\ldots\). Find \(|X\cup Y|\).
solution: \(X=\{5n-4:1\le n\le2018\}\) (up to 10086), \(Y=\{7m+2:1\le m\le2018\}\) (up to 14128). \(X\cap Y\) needs \(x\equiv1\pmod5\) and \(x\equiv2\pmod7\), i.e. \(x\equiv16\pmod{35}\) by CRT.Within \(X\)'s range \([1,10086]\): \(x=16+35k\le10086\Rightarrow k\le287\), giving 288 common terms.\[|X\cup Y|=2018+2018-288=3748\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Turn \(X\cap Y\) into a modular-arithmetic (CRT) problem — find the single residue class both APs share, then count how many of those fall inside the shorter AP's range.
subject: math

question: Let \(AP(a;d)\) denote an infinite A.P. with first term \(a\) and common difference \(d>0\). If \(AP(1;3)\cap AP(2;5)\cap AP(3;7)=AP(a;d)\), find \(a+d\).
solution: Since \(3,5,7\) are pairwise coprime, the intersection is an AP with \(d=\mathrm{lcm}(3,5,7)=105\). Find the smallest common term: solve \(x\equiv1\!\!\pmod3,\ x\equiv2\!\!\pmod5,\ x\equiv3\!\!\pmod7\) by CRT, giving \(x\equiv52\pmod{105}\).\[a=52,\ d=105\Rightarrow a+d=157\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: The intersection of several APs with pairwise-coprime common differences is itself an AP whose common difference is their lcm — find the smallest shared term via CRT.
subject: math

question: Find the sum of \(n\) terms of the series \(1\cdot3^2+2\cdot5^2+3\cdot7^2+\cdots\)
solution: The \(k\)th term is \(k(2k+1)^2=4k^3+4k^2+k\). Summing with the standard closed forms:\[S_n=4\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2+4\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6+\frac{n(n+1)}2=\frac{n(n+1)(6n^2+14n+7)}{6}\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Expand the \(k\)th term into separate powers of \(k\) first, then apply \(\sum k,\sum k^2,\sum k^3\) to each piece and recombine — don't try to spot a pattern by hand.
subject: math

question: If \(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{20}\) are 20 arithmetic means inserted between 13 and 67, find the maximum value among them.
solution: With 20 means, the full run \(13,a_1,\ldots,a_{20},67\) is an AP of 22 terms, so \(d=\dfrac{67-13}{21}=\dfrac{18}{7}\). The largest mean is \(a_{20}\) (closest to 67):\[a_{20}=13+20d=13+\frac{360}7=\frac{451}7\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Inserting \(n\) means between two numbers always makes a run of \(n+2\) terms — count the total terms carefully before computing \(d\).
subject: math

question: If \(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n\) are in H.P., show what \(a_1a_2+a_2a_3+\cdots+a_{n-1}a_n\) equals.
solution: Let \(b_k=1/a_k\), so \(b_1,\ldots,b_n\) is an AP with common difference \(d\). Then \(a_ka_{k+1}=\dfrac1{b_kb_{k+1}}=\dfrac1d\left(\dfrac1{b_k}-\dfrac1{b_{k+1}}\right)=\dfrac1d(a_k-a_{k+1})\). Summing telescopes:\[\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}a_ka_{k+1}=\frac1d(a_1-a_n)\]Since \(d=\dfrac{1/a_n-1/a_1}{n-1}=\dfrac{a_1-a_n}{(n-1)a_1a_n}\), this simplifies to \((n-1)a_1a_n\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Convert the HP to its reciprocal AP first — the telescoping trick that works for \(\tfrac1{r(r+1)}\)-type sums applies directly once you're back in AP-land.
subject: math

question: Three numbers \(a,b,c\) lie between 2 and 18 with sum 25. The numbers \(2,a,b\) are in A.P. and \(b,c,18\) are in G.P. Find \(a+b+c\).
solution: The sum \(a+b+c\) is given directly in the problem as 25 — the AP and GP conditions only pin down the individual values of \(a,b,c\), which this question doesn't ask for.
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Before setting up equations from the AP/GP conditions, check whether the question is actually asking for something already stated outright.
subject: math

question: If the 4th, 10th and 16th terms of a G.P. are \(x,y,z\) respectively, what relation do \(x,y,z\) satisfy?
solution: The indices \(4,10,16\) are equally spaced (gap 6), so \(x,y,z\) themselves form a GP with common ratio \(r^6\). For any GP, the middle term squared equals the product of its neighbors:\[y^2=xz\]
answer: y² = xz  (x, y, z are in G.P.)
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Equally-spaced terms of a GP (same index gap) always form their own GP — check the index gaps before doing any algebra.
subject: math

question: If \(S_n\) is the sum of \(n\) terms of a G.P. with first term \(a\) and common ratio \(r\), find \(S_n:S_{2n}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Factor \(r^{2n}-1\) as \((r^n-1)(r^n+1)\) — the \(S_n\) piece cancels cleanly, leaving a one-term ratio.
subject: math

question: The third term of a G.P. is 9. Find the product of its first five terms.
solution: The product of 5 consecutive GP terms centered on the third term equals that term raised to the 5th power:\[(a_3)^5=9^5=59049\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Same shortcut as before — product of an odd run of GP terms is (middle term)^(count), regardless of what the actual first term or ratio are.
subject: math

question: Find \(3+5+7+\cdots\) to \(n\) terms.
solution: This is an AP with \(a=3,\,d=2\):\[S_n=\frac n2\big[2(3)+(n-1)(2)\big]=\frac n2(2n+4)=n(n+2)\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Plug directly into \(S_n=\tfrac n2[2a+(n-1)d]\) — this series doesn't need any trick, just careful substitution.
subject: math

question: The 5th term of an A.P. is 23 and the 12th term is 58. Find the first term and common difference, hence find \(S_{20}\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Two term conditions give two equations in \(a,d\) — subtract them to eliminate \(a\) first, exactly as you would for simultaneous linear equations.
subject: math

question: A G.P. has first term 12 and sum to infinity 16. Find the common ratio, and hence the sum of the first 6 terms.
solution: \(\dfrac{a}{1-r}=16\) with \(a=12\Rightarrow1-r=\dfrac{12}{16}=\dfrac34\Rightarrow r=\dfrac14\).\[S_6=\frac{12\left(1-(1/4)^6\right)}{1-1/4}=16\left(1-\frac1{4096}\right)=\frac{4095}{256}\]
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Find \(r\) from the sum-to-infinity condition first — then it's a routine finite-GP-sum calculation.
subject: math

question: A ball is dropped from a height of 10 m. After each bounce it rises to \(\tfrac35\) of the height it fell from. Find the total distance travelled before it comes to rest.
solution: Distance \(=10+2\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}10\left(\frac35\right)^n=10+20\cdot\frac{3/5}{1-3/5}=10+20\cdot\frac32=10+30=40\text{ m}\)
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Every bounce after the first contributes twice its rise height (up and back down) — set up the infinite GP for the rises, then double it before adding the initial drop.

question: Find \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(2r-1)(2r+1)}\)
solution: \(\dfrac1{(2r-1)(2r+1)}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1{2r-1}-\dfrac1{2r+1}\right)\), which telescopes to \(\dfrac12\left(1-\dfrac1{2n+1}\right)=\dfrac{n}{2n+1}\)
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Any \(\tfrac1{(\text{linear})(\text{linear}+2)}\) shape splits the same way as \(\tfrac1{r(r+1)}\) — just with a factor of \(\tfrac12\) out front.

question: If \(a+b=10\) with \(a,b>0\), find the maximum possible value of \(ab\).
solution: By AM–GM, \(\dfrac{a+b}2\ge\sqrt{ab}\Rightarrow5\ge\sqrt{ab}\Rightarrow ab\le25\), with equality when \(a=b=5\).
tip: 💡 Quick tip: Fixed-sum, maximize-product questions are AM–GM in disguise — the maximum always occurs when all the terms are equal.

question: Find the 4th term of the H.P. \(\dfrac12,\dfrac15,\dfrac18,\ldots\)

tip: 💡 Quick tip: Always invert an HP into its AP first — never try to spot a pattern in the fractions directly.
